title: It’s Not Hate. It’s Something Harder to Admit.
excerpt: Most people aren’t uncomfortable around differently-abled people because they’re cruel.
body:
Most people aren’t uncomfortable around differently-abled people because they’re cruel.

They’re uncomfortable because they don’t know what to do.

They don’t know whether to offer help, ask questions, or pretend nothing is different. So instead, they create distance.

That distance may seem harmless.

But to the person on the receiving end, it can feel incredibly lonely.

I’ve spent my life watching people change the moment they notice my wheelchair.

Some avoid eye contact.

Some speak to the person beside me instead of speaking to me.

Others become overly cautious, afraid they’ll say the wrong thing.

For a long time, I wondered if there was something wrong with me.

There wasn’t.

The problem wasn’t me.

It was unfamiliarity.

No one is born uncomfortable around differently-abled people.

Children prove that every day.

They ask honest questions. They’re curious, not judgmental. They don’t see someone who needs pity — they simply see someone who is different.

Then society teaches them that disability is something not to talk about.

Don’t stare.

Don’t ask questions.

Don’t bring it up.

So people grow up without ever learning how to interact naturally with differently-abled people. When they finally do, uncertainty replaces confidence.

I don’t believe most people have bad intentions.

I believe they’re afraid of making a mistake.

They’re worried they’ll offend someone.

They’re unsure whether they should help.

Ironically, that fear often creates the very thing they’re trying to avoid: exclusion.

Sometimes saying hello is better than saying nothing at all.

There is another reason we rarely talk about.

Meeting a differently-abled person reminds us that life is fragile.

An accident.

An illness.

A diagnosis.

In a single moment, anyone’s life can change.

That’s an uncomfortable truth.

Sometimes people aren’t reacting to the person in front of them.

They’re reacting to what that person reminds them about themselves.

Here’s the truth.

Differently-abled people don’t expect perfection.

We don’t expect everyone to know the right words.

We simply want to be treated like human beings.

If you’re unsure whether someone needs help, ask.

If they say no, respect that.

If you’re curious, ask respectfully.

Most of us would rather answer an honest question than be avoided because someone was too afraid to start a conversation.

The greatest barriers aren’t always stairs or heavy doors.

Sometimes they’re assumptions.

Sometimes they’re silence.

Sometimes they’re the invisible wall that forms when people don’t know how to interact with someone who is different.

The good news is that invisible walls can be broken.

It starts with something remarkably simple.

A smile.

A conversation.

A willingness to see the person before the wheelchair, the diagnosis, or the label.

Because behind every differently-abled person is exactly what has always been there:

A human being.

Not waiting to be pitied.

Not waiting to inspire you.

Simply waiting to be seen.

With love and light,

Ronahi Zebari
Founder & CEO, Light Upon Light
